title: Adding and subtracting coplanar vectors
prior_knowledge_summary: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude only.
A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction.
A complete vector report includes magnitude, unit and direction.
Students can recognise familiar vectors such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum.
new_learning: A vector arrow represents magnitude by its length and direction by its arrowhead.
Coplanar vectors can be added by placing them head-to-tail and drawing the resultant from the first tail to the final head.
Collinear vectors in opposite directions are combined by subtracting their magnitudes and retaining the direction of the larger vector.
The resultant of two perpendicular vectors can be calculated from the completed right-angled vector triangle.
Subtracting a vector means reversing that vector and then adding it.
not_yet_taught: Resolving a vector into perpendicular components.
Using component equations to combine vectors at arbitrary angles.
Applications belonging to later Physics topics.

visual_planning.reason: Six planned figures make arrow meaning, head-to-tail addition, collinear cancellation, perpendicular calculation, subtraction by reversal and a common construction error visible without introducing Lesson 11 component resolution.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Where does the second arrow begin?
content: A map instruction gives two moves: 6.0 km east, then 8.0 km north. If both arrows are drawn from the same starting point, neither arrow shows where the second move actually begins.
The northward move begins where the eastward move ends. Sliding the second arrow so that its tail meets the first arrow's head produces one continuous journey.
The single arrow from the original start to the final point is the resultant. Its length and direction describe the combined effect of both vectors.

figure.purpose: Create the need for head-to-tail placement by contrasting an unconnected pair of arrows with the actual two-stage route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. On the left, draw 6.0 km east and 8.0 km north arrows incorrectly sharing one tail, with a question mark between them. On the right, slide the north arrow to the east arrow's head and mark the original start and final point. Do not calculate or label the resultant value.
figure.alt_text: A northward vector is moved to the head of an eastward vector so that the arrows show one continuous route.

blocks.title: Read and move a vector arrow without changing it
content: Lesson 9 defined a vector quantity as a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction. On a vector diagram, arrow length represents magnitude and the arrowhead represents direction.
A vector may be slid parallel to itself on the page. It remains the same vector if its length and direction stay unchanged. Do not rotate it, stretch it or reverse its arrowhead while moving it.
For a scale drawing, choose and state one scale, such as 1 cm represents 2 N. Draw each arrow at the correct scale length and measured direction.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction

figure.purpose: Separate a legal parallel translation of a vector arrow from changes that alter the vector.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison strip with four copies of one arrow. Tick a parallel slide with unchanged length and direction. Cross a rotated arrow, a stretched arrow and a reversed arrow. Use colour only to distinguish unchanged from changed properties and keep labels sparse.
figure.alt_text: Only sliding an arrow parallel to itself preserves both its magnitude and direction.

blocks.title: Add vectors head-to-tail
content: To add vector A and vector B, draw A first. Place the tail of B at the head of A while preserving B's length and direction.
Draw the resultant R from the tail of A to the head of B. The resultant arrow points from the original start to the final point, not back toward the start.
The same rule works if B is drawn first and A second. The intermediate route changes, but the first and final points give the same resultant. This is a useful diagram check.
For more than two vectors, continue the chain head-to-tail. One resultant joins the first tail to the final head.

figure.purpose: Show the complete head-to-tail construction and the order check for vector addition.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with two panels. First panel shows A then B head-to-tail and R from the first tail to final head. Second panel shows B then A forming the other sides of a parallelogram and the same R. Use blue for A, orange for B and green for R. No components or coordinate axes.
figure.alt_text: Vectors A and B form a head-to-tail chain, and either order gives the same resultant from start to finish.

blocks.title: Combine vectors on one line
content: Consider a 18 N force east and a 7 N force west. Draw both directions before doing arithmetic. The vectors oppose one another, so their effects partly cancel.
Choose east as positive. The combined vector is $+18\,\mathrm{N}+(-7\,\mathrm{N})=+11\,\mathrm{N}$, so the resultant is 11 N east.
A second way is to subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger: $18-7=11$ N. The direction is east because the larger vector points east.
Independent check: opposing vectors must give a magnitude smaller than 18 N but greater than 0 N. The result 11 N passes that check.

figure.purpose: Connect signed one-line arithmetic with physical cancellation and the direction of the larger vector.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout. Top row shows an 18 N east arrow and a shorter 7 N west arrow. Middle row shows signed arithmetic with east positive. Bottom row shows an 11 N east resultant and a simple bound 0 N less than R less than 18 N. Keep the arithmetic visible and uncluttered.
figure.alt_text: An 18 newton east vector and a 7 newton west vector combine to give 11 newtons east.

blocks.title: Complete a right-angled vector triangle
content: Return to the 6.0 km east and 8.0 km north journey. The given vectors are already perpendicular, so their head-to-tail diagram is a right-angled triangle. No vector has been split into components.
The resultant magnitude is the hypotenuse: $R=\sqrt{(6.0\,\mathrm{km})^2+(8.0\,\mathrm{km})^2}=10.0\,\mathrm{km}$.
Let $\theta$ be measured north of east. Then $\tan\theta=8.0/6.0$, so $\theta=53.1^\circ$. The resultant is 10.0 km at $53.1^\circ$ north of east.
Independent checks: the hypotenuse must be longer than 8.0 km but shorter than $6.0+8.0=14.0$ km, and the larger northward vector makes the angle greater than $45^\circ$. Both checks pass.

figure.purpose: Model a complete perpendicular-vector calculation with direction, units and independent magnitude and angle checks.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated worked triangle. Show 6.0 km east followed head-to-tail by 8.0 km north, with R from start to finish and theta at the start. Beside it, show the Pythagoras line, tangent line and two short check boxes. Do not show any component-resolution arrows.
figure.alt_text: A right-angled vector triangle combines 6.0 kilometres east and 8.0 kilometres north into 10.0 kilometres at 53.1 degrees north of east.

blocks.title: Subtract by reversing one arrow
content: Vector subtraction is not ordinary subtraction of two magnitudes. To find $\vec{A}-\vec{B}$, reverse vector B to make $-\vec{B}$, then add $\vec{A}+(-\vec{B})$ head-to-tail.
Let A be 9.0 m east and B be 4.0 m north. Then $\vec{A}-\vec{B}$ is 9.0 m east added to 4.0 m south.
The completed right-angled triangle gives $R=\sqrt{9.0^2+4.0^2}=9.85$ m and $\theta=\tan^{-1}(4.0/9.0)=24.0^\circ$ south of east.
The same reversal rule works on one line. If C is 11 N east and D is 6 N east, then $\vec{C}-\vec{D}$ becomes 11 N east plus 6 N west, giving 5 N east.

Independent check: changing from addition to subtraction reverses only B. The northward part must therefore become southward, while the eastward part remains eastward. The answer has exactly those directions.

figure.purpose: Make subtraction operational by showing B reversed before it is added to A.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper three-stage teacher sketch. Stage 1 shows A east and B north. Stage 2 flips B to minus B south without changing its length. Stage 3 places minus B at A's head and draws the southeast resultant from the original start. Include the 9.85 m and 24.0 degree result only in a small worked side panel.
figure.alt_text: Subtracting a northward vector reverses it southward before adding it head-to-tail to an eastward vector.

blocks.title: Why adding magnitudes often gives the wrong answer
content: It can feel natural to add every numerical magnitude because ordinary numbers have no direction. That works only when vectors point along the same line in the same direction.
For perpendicular or oblique vectors, the head-to-tail triangle controls the result. The resultant is not normally the sum of the two magnitudes, and it must include a direction.

A second common error is to draw the resultant between the two arrowheads when both vectors share a tail. That connecting arrow represents a difference between the vectors. For addition, first make a head-to-tail chain, then draw from the first tail to the final head.

For an oblique pair, a careful scale drawing gives both magnitude and direction without resolving either vector. State the scale, preserve each direction, complete the head-to-tail triangle, then measure the resultant.

blocks.title: Start with direction, then choose the shortest valid route
content: For any coplanar vector problem, draw or imagine the arrow directions before calculating. Keep magnitude, unit and direction together in the final result.
Use signed addition for collinear vectors, Pythagoras and tangent when the given vectors are perpendicular, and a head-to-tail scale drawing for an arbitrary angle.
For subtraction, reverse the vector being subtracted and then use the same addition methods.
This lesson combines complete vectors. The next lesson will teach how one vector can be resolved into perpendicular components, so that later method is not used here.
